interviewQuestions.question: Tell me about a time you disagreed with your manager.
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
My manager wanted to roll a billing-related feature flag out to 100% of users in one step to hit a launch date. I proposed staging it — 5%, then 25%, then 100% over three days — because a bad bug at full rollout meant refund processing for our entire user base instead of a small slice.

I made the case with a concrete cost comparison rather than just a gut feeling: at 5% a bug affects roughly 2,000 accounts and is cheap to remediate manually; at 100% it's the full base and needs an automated refund pipeline we didn't have yet. She agreed to a compressed two-day version of the staged plan that still hit the launch date.

On day one, at 5%, we caught a currency-rounding bug that would have silently overcharged fractions of a cent on every international transaction — invisible at small scale, but it would have generated thousands of support tickets at 100%. We fixed it same-day and finished the rollout on schedule.

What I took from it: the disagreement wasn't about being right in the abstract, it was about giving both of us a way to verify who was right before the cost of being wrong got large. That's the version of pushback I try to bring every time — not just an opinion, but a plan that surfaces the truth cheaply.

**Testing:** whether you can push back with evidence and a workable compromise, rather than either deferring immediately or digging in past the point of usefulness.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Disagreement

interviewQuestions.question: Tell me about a time you influenced a decision without having any authority over the people involved.
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Our team's deploys were breaking another team's downstream service roughly once a month, because we didn't publish a changelog for schema changes to an internal API they consumed. I had no authority over either team's roadmap or headcount.

I started by writing up the last three incidents with their actual cost attached — about six engineer-hours of cross-team debugging each time, pulled from incident postmortems, not estimated after the fact. Then I proposed a specific, cheap fix: a CI check that fails a pull request if it changes our API's schema without a corresponding changelog entry.

Before taking it to either team's lead, I got one senior engineer on the downstream team to co-review the proposal. That mattered more than the technical design — when I did bring it to both leads, it wasn't "my idea," it was something a person on the affected team had already validated as solving their actual pain. Both teams adopted it within two weeks; it's been running eight months with zero repeat incidents of that kind.

The part I'd emphasize to anyone trying this: the persuasion work happens with your peers before it happens with anyone who can say yes on paper. By the time you reach the person with formal authority to approve it, you want them ratifying something the affected humans already want, not evaluating a cold pitch.

**Testing:** whether you understand influence as a peer-credibility process, not a top-down pitch — and whether you can quantify a problem instead of asserting it.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Influence

interviewQuestions.question: What's your proudest achievement, and why that one specifically?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
A data-validation layer I built after tracing three separate production incidents back to the same root cause: malformed events from an upstream service reaching our pipeline unchecked. It's not the biggest project I've worked on by scope, and that's actually why I picked it.

I could point to a larger feature launch I contributed to, but my fingerprint on that one is diffuse — I owned one component among many. This validation layer, I designed and drove end to end: I picked the schema-validation library, decided where in the pipeline to intercept bad events versus reject upstream, and made the call to fail loudly (reject and alert) rather than silently drop or auto-correct malformed data, because silent correction had caused a subtler bug before.

In the year since, it's caught over 200 malformed events before they reached production — each one a potential incident that never happened, which is a harder thing to point to than a shipped feature but a real one. Two other teams independently copied the pattern into their own ingestion pipelines after seeing it in a postmortem review, which is the part I'm actually proudest of: the value didn't stop at my team's boundary.

When picking what to call "proudest," I optimize for where my own judgment call is clearly visible in the outcome, not for the biggest number I can cite.

**Testing:** whether you can identify and defend your own specific contribution, and whether your definition of "proud" tracks real judgment and impact rather than borrowed scale.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Values & impact

interviewQuestions.question: You're interviewing for a staff role and get asked a fairly junior-sounding prompt — "tell me about a conflict with a coworker." How do you make sure your answer lands at the right level?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I don't change the question's category, I change the scope of the story and what I emphasize in it. A junior-level conflict story is often "we disagreed on an implementation detail and worked it out." At staff level, I'd reach for a conflict where the stakes were structural — disagreement over a technical direction that affected multiple teams, or friction with a peer staff engineer over which of two systems should be the long-term source of truth.

Concretely: I once disagreed with another senior engineer over whether a new analytics pipeline should read from our team's existing event stream or stand up a parallel one. The conflict wasn't personal, but it was real — his team had already sunk two months into the parallel design. Rather than simply arguing my design was better, I asked what would make his team confident a shared stream wouldn't become a bottleneck for their use case, then spent a week building a load-test proving our existing stream could absorb their expected volume with headroom. He changed his recommendation once the data was in front of him, and we retired his team's two months of parallel work with his own sign-off, not because I overruled him.

What makes this staff-scoped isn't the STAR mechanics — it's that the conflict crossed team boundaries, involved a peer's sunk cost, and resolved through evidence rather than my title or his conceding to avoid friction.

**Testing:** whether you understand that seniority changes the scope and stakes of the story you select, not the underlying question category or structure.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Calibration
